analysis.one_liner: Requires the President and Vice President to divest financial interests that conflict with their office.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2019 and referred to the House Oversight Committee, where it died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 to require the President and Vice President to sell off, or place in a blind trust, any financial interest that poses a conflict of interest within 30 days of taking office [S3]. It would also force more detailed public disclosure of any business in which the President, Vice President, or their spouse or dependent child holds a significant stake, including the names of other significant owners and details of liabilities and assets worth $10,000 or more [S3]. No such requirement currently applies to the President or Vice President; existing ethics law leaves them outside the conflict-of-interest rules that bind other executive branch officials. The bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would gain clearer assurance that the President and Vice President are not making official decisions while personally invested in the outcome, and government ethics enforcers, who would get defined standards for what counts as a disqualifying interest [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President and Vice President, within 30 days of taking office, to divest financial interests that pose a conflict of interest, either by converting them to non-conflicting investments or placing them in a qualified blind or diversified trust [S3].
Exempts a President or Vice President from divestiture only if they comply with section 102's full disclosure requirements, giving them a compliance path [S3].

Expands public financial disclosures for the President and Vice President to cover any business in which they or a spouse or dependent child hold a significant interest, requiring disclosure of other significant owners, liabilities over $10,000, and assets worth $10,000 or more [S3].
Directs the Office of Government Ethics to write regulations within 120 days defining what counts as a conflict and a 'significant financial interest' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Presidents, Vice Presidents, and their families, who would have to sell or blind-trust business holdings and disclose far more detail about them; a sitting officeholder with extensive business interests would bear the largest cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Presidents and VPs with business holdings

drawbacks.text: The divestiture requirement is broad and could force a President or Vice President to sell assets quickly, potentially at unfavorable prices, which is the standard criticism of mandatory divestiture rules.
The bill relies on the Office of Government Ethics to define key terms like 'significant financial interest,' leaving considerable discretion to regulators in how strictly the rules are applied [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — removing the possibility that a sitting President personally profits from official decisions — is substantial, and the cost falls almost entirely on the officeholders themselves, who can comply by selling, using trusts, or full disclosure. The main design question is how regulators define the threshold terms, but the trade-off strongly favors disclosure and divestiture.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Oversight and Reform Committee the day it was introduced and never advanced further; it received no hearing and no vote before the 116th Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Katherine Clark of Massachusetts introduced the Presidential Accountability Act on March 4, 2019, joined by Representative Pramila Jayapal [S1][S3].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Reform [S5].
That referral was the bill's last action; the committee took it up no further and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting Presidents and Vice Presidents with business holdings — and any future officeholder whose family profits from their official position — are better off because the bill never advanced, since no divestiture or expanded disclosure requirement was ever enacted.

for.name: Rep. Katherine Clark (D-MA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require presidential and vice-presidential divestiture of conflicting financial interests [S1][S3].

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-WA)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor [S4].

against.name: House Committee on Oversight and Reform
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill's two supporters were both Democrats (the sponsor plus one of 231 House Democrats as cosponsor), and no Republican support is recorded in the bill's history [S4].

industries.note: Any business in which the President, Vice President, or their spouse or dependent child held a significant interest would face mandatory divestiture or far deeper public disclosure, including other significant owners and liabilities over $10,000 [S3]. The bill's cost falls entirely on these officeholders and their enterprises, which currently face no comparable requirement.
